indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.4.2.2: Know the functions and assemblage of basic electronics components
indicator.objective: Investigate the function of batteries in electronic devices

skills.description: Understand that a battery stores and provides electrical energy to make a device work
Identify common devices that use batteries
Describe what happens when a battery is removed or dead
Understand that a battery must be connected in a complete loop to work

misconceptions: Any battery can work in any device.
A wire alone can light a bulb without a battery.
Batteries are only found in phones.
If a device doesn't work, it is always broken; it never just needs a new battery.

questions.stem: Which of these devices needs a battery to work?
options: A television plugged into the wall
hints: You can carry it around.
It uses small cells inside.
questions.explanation: A torch uses batteries to work, making it portable.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all devices need wall sockets.

questions.stem: What is the job of a battery in a device?
options: To provide energy for the device to work
To change the colour of the device
hints: It stores power.
Without it, the device won't work.
questions.explanation: A battery stores and provides electrical energy to make the device work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know what a battery actually does.

questions.stem: What happens to a torch when you take out its batteries?
hints: The battery gives it energy.
No battery, no power.
questions.explanation: Without the batteries, the torch has no source of energy and will not light up.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a torch can work without a battery.

questions.stem: Which of these common household items uses a battery?
hints: You use it to change TV channels.
It is small and you hold it.
questions.explanation: A remote control uses batteries to send signals to the TV.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think of small devices as using batteries.

questions.stem: What do we call a device that stores electrical energy?
hints: You put it in a torch.
It has positive and negative ends.
questions.explanation: A battery stores electrical energy for use in devices.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wires store energy.

questions.stem: Ama has a toy car that won't move. She checks inside and sees it needs batteries. What should she do?
hints: It needs energy to move.
Batteries provide energy.
questions.explanation: The toy car needs batteries to get energy to move. Putting in new batteries should make it work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the toy is permanently broken.

questions.stem: Why does a torch stop shining after a long time of use?
options: The battery runs out of energy
hints: Batteries don't last forever.
It loses its stored power.
questions.explanation: The battery stores a limited amount of energy. After it runs out, the torch stops shining.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the bulb itself 'wears out' instantly.

questions.stem: To make a bulb light up using a battery and a wire, what must you do?
options: Connect only one end of the wire
Make a complete loop connecting the battery and bulb
Just place the wire on the table
hints: The electricity needs a path.
The loop must go all the way around.
questions.explanation: Electricity must flow in a complete loop (circuit) from the battery to the bulb and back again for it to light up.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think one connection is enough.

questions.stem: Which of these devices does NOT use a battery?
options: A television plugged into the wall
hints: It is plugged into a wall socket.
It is large and not portable.
questions.explanation: A television plugged into the wall uses electricity from the mains, not a battery.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all electronics use batteries.

questions.stem: Why do we put batteries in a flashlight instead of plugging it into a wall?
options: Because it needs to be portable and used anywhere
hints: You carry a flashlight around.
You might need it when there is no wall socket.
questions.explanation: Batteries make a flashlight portable so you can carry it anywhere, even without a power outlet.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the concept of portability.

questions.stem: What is needed to make electricity flow in a simple circuit?
hints: It must be a full circle.
No breaks in the path.
questions.explanation: Electricity needs a complete, unbroken loop to flow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think broken circuits work.

questions.stem: Name one device in your home that uses batteries.
hints: Look around your living room.
What small device do you carry around?
questions.explanation: Common devices include torches, remote controls, watches, and radios.

questions.stem: Ama puts a battery into a torch the wrong way round. The torch does not light. Why?
options: The battery must be inserted correctly for the circuit to complete
The torch is afraid of the dark
hints: Batteries have positive and negative ends.
They must line up correctly.
questions.explanation: Batteries must be placed in the correct direction to connect the circuit properly and let electricity flow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you can put a battery in any way.

questions.stem: Why does a bulb go off if you cut the wire in a simple circuit?
options: Because the electricity can no longer flow in a complete loop
Because the wire is too long
hints: A cut wire breaks the path.
Electricity needs a continuous loop.
questions.explanation: Cutting the wire breaks the circuit, stopping the flow of electricity, so the bulb goes off.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cutting the wire destroys the electricity.

questions.stem: What does it mean when we say a battery is 'flat'?
options: It is physically flat in shape
It has run out of stored electrical energy
It is too big for the device
hints: It cannot power the device anymore.
You need to recharge or replace it.
questions.explanation: A 'flat' or 'dead' battery has used up its stored energy and cannot power the device.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think flat refers to the shape.

questions.stem: Which two components would you need to make a simple flashlight?
options: A battery, a bulb, and a wire (to make a circuit)
A bulb and a wire only
hints: You need power, a light, and a path.
The electricity needs to flow from one to the other.
questions.explanation: You need a battery (power), a bulb (light), and a wire (to make the complete circuit for electricity to flow).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you just need a battery and a bulb touching.

questions.stem: Explain why a toy car will not move if the batteries are removed.

criteria.description: States that the batteries provide the energy
States that without batteries, the circuit is broken and electricity cannot flow

hints: What is the job of the batteries?
No power means no movement.
questions.explanation: Batteries provide the energy for the toy car. Without them, there is no source of electricity to complete the circuit and power the motor.

questions.stem: A student connects a wire to the positive end of a battery, then touches the other end of the wire to the same positive end. Will the bulb light up?
options: No, because the circuit is not complete (it bypasses the bulb and goes back to the same end)
Yes, if the battery is new
It depends on the colour of the wire
hints: The electricity needs to go through the bulb.
Connecting both ends to the same side does not make a complete loop through the bulb.
questions.explanation: The circuit is not complete. To light the bulb, the wire must go from one end of the battery, through the bulb, and back to the other end of the battery.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think touching a wire to a battery is enough.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to leave dead batteries in a device for a very long time?

criteria.description: States that dead batteries can leak acid or chemicals
States that this can damage the device or be harmful to the user

hints: Dead batteries can 'leak' over time.
It is not good to leave them inside.
questions.explanation: Old batteries can leak corrosive chemicals, which can ruin the device and be harmful if touched.

questions.stem: Using a battery, a bulb, and a wire, show your teacher how to make the bulb light up.

criteria.description: Connects one end of the wire to one end of the battery
Connects the other end of the wire to the other end of the battery
Successfully creates a complete circuit and lights the bulb

hints: Make sure the wire touches the metal parts.
Form a full loop.
questions.explanation: This demonstrates understanding of a simple circuit and the function of a battery as a power source.
